# Topic 1 — Ordinal or multinomial? {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## A decision

| Question | Answer | Model |
|---|---|---|
| Is there a **meaningful order**? | No | **Multinomial** logistic |
| | Yes | **Ordinal** logistic (proportional odds) |
| Does **proportional odds** hold (Brant, cut-point ORs)? | Yes | one OR per predictor |
| | One or a few predictors fail | **Partial** proportional odds |
| | Many fail | **Multinomial** |

## The same data, two models

```{r}
a_ord <- MASS::polr(anaemia ~ wealth + tribal, data = mat, Hess = TRUE)
a_mn <- nnet::multinom(factor(anaemia, ordered = FALSE) ~ wealth + tribal, data = mat, trace = FALSE)
c(ordinal = AIC(a_ord), multinomial = AIC(a_mn)) |> round(0)
```

::: {.key}
The multinomial model has the **lower AIC** because it frees the tribal effect at each cut-point; it also needs **many more parameters** (`r length(coef(a_mn))` vs `r length(coef(a_ord)) + length(a_ord$zeta)`). When proportional odds **holds**, the ordinal model is simpler and **more powerful**. When it fails and cannot be relaxed, **multinomial is the safe fallback**.
:::

# Topic 2 — Showing results {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Probabilities against a predictor

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-height: 4
m_ord <- MASS::polr(anaemia ~ wealth + education + bmi + anc_visits + parity + age + tribal + residence, data = mat, Hess = TRUE)
nd <- data.frame(wealth = 1:5, education = factor("Primary", levels = levels(mat$education)), bmi = 20.5, anc_visits = 3, parity = 2, age = 27, tribal = factor("No", levels = c("No", "Yes")), residence = factor("Rural", levels = c("Urban", "Rural")))
cbind(wealth = 1:5, as.data.frame(predict(m_ord, newdata = nd, type = "probs"))) |> pivot_longer(-wealth, names_to = "anaemia", values_to = "probability") |>
  mutate(anaemia = factor(anaemia, levels = levels(mat$anaemia))) |>
  ggplot(aes(wealth, probability, colour = anaemia)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + labs(x = "Wealth quintile", y = "Predicted probability", colour = NULL)
```

The same idea for the nominal outcome: predicted probabilities of each **delivery place** across wealth show **home falling and private rising**.

## Accuracy is a weak summary

```{r}
mat$delivery <- relevel(mat$delivery, ref = "Home")
mn <- nnet::multinom(delivery ~ wealth + education + anc_visits + residence + tribal, data = mat, trace = FALSE)
c(model = mean(predict(mn) == mat$delivery), always_most_common = max(prop.table(table(mat$delivery)))) |> round(2)
```

::: {.warn}
The model is right about **48%** of the time vs **32%** for always guessing the most common place. Covariates **shift probabilities** but **cannot predict an individual's choice**; accuracy ignores the probabilities. Use **predicted probabilities**, **AIC** or **log-likelihood**, and, if prediction is the aim, **calibration** and **proper scoring rules**.
:::

# Topic 3 — Reporting {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Wording

::: {.good}
**Ordinal:** "In a proportional-odds model adjusted for education, BMI, antenatal visits, parity, age, tribal group and residence, each higher wealth quintile was associated with **24% lower odds** of being in a worse anaemia category (OR 0.76, 95% CI ...). The assumption held for all predictors except tribal group, so its effect is reported separately at each cut-point."
:::

::: {.good}
**Multinomial:** "Compared with home delivery, each wealth quintile increased the **relative risk** of delivering in a private hospital 2.8-fold (RRR 2.76, 95% CI ...)."
:::

## Reporting checklist

::: {.incremental}
1. **Outcome** categories, order, **counts**; **reference** category (nominal)
2. **Model** and **why** (ordered or not); **software** (`MASS`, `nnet`, `ordinal`)
3. **Odds ratios** (ordinal) or **relative risk ratios** (multinomial) with **95% CI**; adjustment set
4. **Assumption check** (Brant, cut-specific ORs) and what you did
5. **Predicted probabilities** for key profiles
6. **Limitations**: sparse categories, many parameters, association not cause, self-reported outcomes
:::

## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s5q1", "When is the multinomial model a good choice for an ordered outcome?",
         c("The sample of women is very small for a model with many parameters",
           "All the predictors in the model are binary variables only",
           "Proportional odds fails for many predictors and cannot be relaxed",
           "The outcome has three ordered categories in the data set"), answer = 3,
         explain = "Multinomial makes no ordering assumption, so it is the fallback when proportional odds clearly fails. It uses more parameters and so needs a larger sample.")
```

## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s5q2", "The multinomial model classifies 48% of women correctly and always guessing the most common place gives 32%. What is the best conclusion?",
         c("The model is excellent, since it beats guessing the most common place",
           "Covariates shift probabilities, but accuracy is a weak summary",
           "The model has failed and should be rejected for this use",
           "The two numbers cannot be compared with each other in any way"), answer = 2,
         explain = "Even a useful model may predict an individual's category poorly. Accuracy ignores the predicted probabilities, so judge the model by probabilities, likelihood and calibration.")
```

## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s5q3", "Why plot predicted probabilities against a predictor such as wealth?",
         c("They give the p-value of the Brant test for the predictor shown",
           "They replace the need for odds ratios in any paper that is written",
           "They show how each category's probability changes with it",
           "They prove that the effect of the predictor is a causal one"), answer = 3,
         explain = "The plot shows what the model implies for readers on the probability scale: for example home deliveries falling and private rising.")
```

## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s5q4", "Which sentence is the best way to report an ordinal result when the assumption holds?",
         c("Each higher quintile lowers the anaemia grade by 0.76 of one whole category",
           "Wealthy women have 76% of the anaemia that is found in poor women",
           "Wealth had a significant effect on anaemia because the p-value was small",
           "Each higher quintile went with 24% lower odds of a worse category (OR 0.76)"), answer = 4,
         explain = "State the OR for a higher category with its CI and the adjustment. Avoid treating categories as numbers or giving only a p-value.")
```

## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s5q5", "What belongs in the limitations of a categorical-outcome analysis?",
         c("Sparse categories, many parameters, and association not being cause",
           "The fact that the outcome has more than two categories to model",
           "That odds ratios cannot be reported when there are many categories",
           "That the software used for the analysis was written in the R language"), answer = 1,
         explain = "Small categories and many parameters destabilise estimates, and an observational design supports association only.")
```

## Score and take-home

**Your score: <span class="quiz-score"></span>**

::: {.incremental}
- Ordered and the assumption holds: **ordinal**; fails for one or two: **partial**; many or no order: **multinomial**
- Show **predicted probabilities** and plots, not only odds ratios
- Do not judge by **classification accuracy**
- Report **categories, reference, model, ORs/RRRs with CI, assumption check, limitations**
:::
